opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a lot, and I want to be careful, because it's easy to overclaim in either direction. The way I'd frame it is that both systems are solving a similar problem under similar pressures, so it's not that surprising that some similar structure falls out.

Think about what a language model is being trained to do. It's predicting the next token across an enormous amount of human-generated text. And to do that well, really well, you can't just memorize surface statistics. At some point the cheapest way to predict what a person will say next is to build some internal model of the things people are talking about, and of the person doing the talking. So the training objective pushes the model toward representations that compress the world the way human language compresses it. And human language is itself an artifact of human cognition. It's carved at the joints that our brains found useful. So in a sense the model is reverse-engineering the structure of human thought from its exhaust.

On the human side, there's a long line of thinking in neuroscience, predictive processing and the free energy work, that says the brain is fundamentally a prediction machine too. You're constantly generating expectations about incoming sensory data and updating on the error. That's not the same as next-token prediction, the brain is embodied, it's multimodal, it's acting in the world, but the core move of minimizing prediction error by building a generative model is shared.

So when we look inside these models with interpretability tools and find things like features that correspond to concepts, abstractions that generalize across languages, something that looks like planning ahead a few tokens, or representations of space and time that are roughly linear, I don't read that as the model secretly being a brain. I read it as convergent evolution. Different substrates, a similar optimization target, and a shared data source, so you get some shared solutions.

Where I'd push back on the analogy is the architecture and the learning process. Humans learn from a tiny amount of data compared to these models, we have persistent memory, we have a body and drives and a continuous stream of experience. LLMs, at least the classic ones, are trained once, run as a forward pass, and don't have that ongoing loop with the world. So I think the honest answer is that the similarities tell us something real about what good solutions to modeling the world look like, and the differences remind us that we shouldn't assume the inner life, or the failure modes, are the same. In many ways the failure modes are where it's most interesting, because when a model hallucinates or gets tripped up by a weird prompt, that tells you exactly where the analogy breaks down.

r001.rationale: The response points to human-generated text and language as an artifact of human cognition, but does not say humans made LLMs in their own image.

r002.rationale: It says prediction can encourage internal models that compress the world, but does not identify information compressibility as what makes learning possible.

r003.rationale: The response discusses compression, but does not state that efficient compression algorithms tend toward a lowest-dimensional solution when one exists.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it is that both systems are, at bottom, prediction engines built on top of a compressed model of the world. The brain is constantly generating expectations about what comes next, whether that's the next word in a sentence, the next visual input, the next thing someone's going to do, and it updates when reality diverges from the prediction. That's the predictive processing story, and it's become pretty mainstream in neuroscience. A language model is doing something structurally very similar: it's been trained to minimize surprise over an enormous stream of human-generated text, and in order to do that well it has to build internal representations of the things that generate that text, which is people, their reasoning, their goals, the physical world they describe.

Where the analogy gets interesting is in what emerges from that pressure. In humans, you don't learn concepts by being handed definitions, you learn them because having the concept makes you better at anticipating the world. Same thing in the model. Nobody wrote a module for "irony" or "causation" or "what a lawyer would say next." Those abstractions show up because they're the most efficient way to compress the data. So you get this layered structure in both cases: low-level feature detection, then mid-level patterns, then high-level abstractions that are reused across wildly different contexts. When interpretability researchers find a single feature in a model that fires for the Golden Gate Bridge whether you mention it in English, in French, or show it a picture, that's very reminiscent of concept cells in the human brain that respond to Jennifer Aniston regardless of whether it's her face or her name.

Now, I want to be careful here, because the analogy is at the level of computational structure, not implementation. Neurons aren't matrix multiplications, the brain has a body and a reward system and runs online in real time, and models get one giant batch of training and then mostly freeze. Those differences matter a lot. But I think people underrate how much the shared objective, predicting well under limited capacity, constrains the solution space. If you have two very different substrates both trying to solve that problem on the same data, you should expect convergent structure, and that's increasingly what we see. The other thing I'd say is that the in-context behavior, what the model does within a single conversation, looks a lot like working memory and attention in the psychological sense. The weights are the long-term knowledge, the context window is the scratchpad, and attention is literally the mechanism deciding what in that scratchpad is relevant right now. That's not a perfect mapping, but it's close enough that I think cognitive science and ML have a lot more to say to each other than either field has fully admitted yet.

r001.rationale: It attributes similarity to shared prediction objectives and convergent structure, not to humans having made LLMs in their own image.

r002.rationale: It says concepts emerge as efficient ways to compress data, but does not state that information’s compressibility is what makes learning possible.

r003.rationale: It discusses efficient compression and shared constraints, but does not say that learning algorithms tend to find a lowest-dimensional solution when one exists.

astra-6.text:
I think the useful analogy is at the level of computation. Humans take in information, build internal representations, and use those representations to make predictions. Language models do something that resembles that: during training, they learn patterns that let them use context to predict what comes next. And doing that well can require representing quite a lot about the world, rather than just learning which words tend to sit next to each other.

But we should distinguish similar behavior from a similar underlying mechanism. If a model makes the same mistake a person makes, that’s interesting, but it doesn’t establish that they arrived there through the same process. You want to ask what information each system is using, how it represents that information, and what happens when you intervene.

So I’d treat the analogy as a source of hypotheses. Could some forms of reasoning emerge from prediction in both systems? Could context shape their behavior in comparable ways? Those are useful questions. They don’t require us to assume that an LLM has human experiences, motivations, or consciousness.

r001.rationale: The response compares computation and prediction in humans and language models, but does not attribute their structural similarity to humans having made LLMs in their own image.

r002.rationale: It discusses learning patterns and representing the world, but does not identify information compressibility as what makes learning possible.

r003.rationale: It does not state that efficient information compression leads learning algorithms to find a lowest-dimensional solution when one exists.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the useful place to start is that both humans and language models learn structure from experience, and then use that structure to make sense of something new. We don’t approach every sentence or every situation from scratch. We bring expectations, associations, and abstractions that shape what we notice and what we think comes next.

In a language model, you can see a version of that in how context changes the interpretation of a word or an idea. The same sentence can mean something quite different depending on what came before it. Human cognition is deeply contextual in that way, too.

But I’d distinguish an analogy in computation from a claim that the underlying experience is the same. Humans have bodies, emotions, motivations, and a continuous history of interacting with the world. So the interesting question is: which cognitive functions can emerge from learning patterns, and which depend on those other ingredients? The similarities give us a way to investigate that; they don’t settle it.

r001.rationale: The response compares how humans and language models learn structure, but does not say that the similarity partly comes from humans building LLMs in their own image.

r002.rationale: It discusses learning structure from experience, but does not identify information compressibility as what makes learning possible.

r003.rationale: It does not describe learning algorithms that efficiently compress information or say they tend toward a lowest-dimensional solution when one exists.
